questions.q: Which Indo-Greek king is famously associated with the Buddhist text *Milindapanha* and ruled from Sagala (modern Sialkot)?
questions.a: Menander I (Milinda), c. 155–130 BCE. A wrong answer (e.g., Demetrius or Eucratides) reveals confusion between the early Bactrian conquerors and the later Indo-Greek rulers who actually governed in India and engaged with Buddhism.

questions.q: Why did the Kushanas adopt the title *devaputra* ("son of god") and install colossal statues in shrines at Mat and Surkh Kotal?
questions.a: To legitimize their rule over a culturally diverse empire by claiming divine descent, a concept borrowed from Chinese "Son of Heaven" ideology and Iranian royal cults, thereby transcending local Indian legitimizing strategies. A wrong answer that says "they were Buddhists so they worshipped Buddha" misses the political theology: the title and statues projected *the king himself* as divine, not the Buddha.

questions.q: A coin hoard found in Punjab contains: (1) Indo-Greek bilingual drachms, (2) Shaka silver coins with Greek/Kharoshthi legends, (3) Kushana gold dinars of Vima Kadphises with Shiva on the reverse, and (4) Roman aurei of Augustus. Arrange these in chronological order of minting and explain what the progression of scripts and deities reveals about the changing political economy of the region.
questions.a: Chronology: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 (Roman coins arrive later via trade). The shift from bilingual Greek/Kharoshthi to exclusively Indian deities (Shiva) on Kushana gold shows increasing localization of foreign rulers and the growing importance of Indian Ocean trade (Roman gold). A student who orders them randomly or ignores the deity shift fails to connect numismatic evidence to political assimilation and trade dynamics.

questions.q: Compare the Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman (c. 150 CE) with the Allahabad Pillar inscription of Samudragupta (c. 350 CE). Both are *prashastis*, but how does Rudradaman's emphasis on repairing the Sudarshana lake *without taxing his subjects* reflect a different model of kingship from the Gupta *samanta* system?
questions.a: Rudradaman, a Shaka Kshatrapa, projects a personal, benevolent monarch who directly maintains infrastructure using his own resources—a Central Asian "great king" ideal. Samudragupta's *prashasti* celebrates conquest and extraction through *samantas*. Confusing the two indicates inability to distinguish between Shaka/Kshatrapa personalist rule and Gupta feudal integration.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "The Indo-Greeks were merely transient invaders who left no lasting legacy in India." Use evidence from coinage, art, astronomy, and Buddhism to support your judgment.
questions.a: The claim is false. Indo-Greeks introduced: (a) die-struck bilingual coins that became the template for all subsequent Indian coinage; (b) Gandhara art (Greco-Buddhist synthesis); (c) Greek astronomical terms (*horā*, *kendra*) in Indian texts; (d) royal patronage of Buddhism (Menander). A student who agrees with the claim overlooks these structural contributions and confuses political disappearance with cultural erasure.

questions.q: Construct a timeline (c. 200 BCE–300 CE) showing the overlapping reigns of the last Indo-Greeks, the Shakas (Northern and Western Kshatrapas), the Parthians (Gondopharids), and the early Kushanas. Annotate three turning points where one group displaced another, and explain the cause in each case (e.g., nomadic pressure, internal feud, trade-route control).
questions.a: Turning points: (1) c. 55 BCE: Azes I (Shaka) ends Indo-Greek rule in Taxila—cause: Scythian migration after Yuezhi pressure. (2) c. 20 CE: Gondophares (Parthian) takes Arachosia/Gandhara—cause: Parthian expansion exploiting Shaka fragmentation. (3) c. 78 CE: Kanishka (Kushana) conquers northwest—cause: Yuezhi unification under Kujula Kadphises. A poor timeline merges groups or misses the nomadic chain reaction.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: 2nd century BCE–3rd century CE saw successive waves of Central Asian groups—Indo-Greeks (Bactrian Greeks), Shakas (Scythians), Parthians, and Kushanas (Yuezhi)—establish kingdoms in ______ and western India, introducing new political ideas (divine kingship, devaputra title), minting the first portrait coins with bilingual legends, patronizing Gandhara and Mathura art, and integrating into Indian society through Buddhism, land grants, and intermarriage.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you are visiting the National Museum in Delhi and see a gold coin with a Greek legend on one side and ______ on the other, showing a king wearing a diadem and a deity on the reverse.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can compare the political chronology, coinage innovations, and cultural contributions of the four groups; explain how each used religion and art to legitimize rule; and assess their impact on trade, urbanization, and the evolution of kingship in post-Mauryan India.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: 2nd century BCE–3rd century CE saw successive waves of Central Asian groups—Indo-Greeks (Bactrian Greeks), Shakas (Scythians), Parthians, and Kushanas (Yuezhi)—establish kingdoms in northwestern and western India, introducing new political ideas (divine kingship, devaputra title), minting the first portrait coins with bilingual legends, patronizing Gandhara and Mathura art, and integrating into Indian society through Buddhism, land grants, and ______.
